overview.title: 📖 Overview: Completing the Night, Beginning the Day
overview.subtitle: Tamid 26a–26b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf completes the account of the ritually impure priest's nighttime journey — through a lamplit underground passage to a chamber with an immersion pool, a warming fire, and a bathroom designed for privacy — before he rejoins his fellow priests until dawn. A new mishna then opens the day's service: whoever wishes to remove the ashes from the altar must immerse before the appointed officer arrives, at an unpredictable hour tied to the rooster's crow, after which a lottery determines who wins the privilege. The Gemara spends the rest of the daf grounding the earlier mishna's details in verses — deriving the three separate priestly guard posts from Numbers 3:38, resolving whether Beit Avtinas and Beit HaNitzotz were true upper stories, and explaining how Beit HaMoked's stone benches were built without violating the prohibition on iron tools in the Temple.

slides.title: 🕯️ The Impure Priest's Path to Purification
slides.subtitle: Completing the account begun on the previous daf

nodes.content: 🚶 He walks through a circuitous underground passage beneath the Temple building — since his impurity bars him from the courtyard itself
🕯️ Lamps burn on both sides of the passage, lighting his way to the Chamber of Immersion
🚪 A private 'bathroom of honor' along the way: a closed door signals occupancy, an open door signals it's free — protecting everyone's privacy
💧 He descends, immerses, ascends, dries himself, and warms up by a fire kept burning there for this purpose

🌅 He returns to sit with his fellow priests until the courtyard gates open at dawn — only then may he leave (his purification isn't complete until sunset, so rabbinically he can't linger during the day)

slides.title: 📜 Deriving Three Guard Posts From One Verse
slides.subtitle: Numbers 3:38, read word by word

steps.content: 1️⃣ Abaye's source: 'those camping before the Tabernacle...were Moses and Aaron and his sons, keeping the watch of the Sanctuary' (Num. 3:38)
2️⃣ Objection: the verse groups Moses (a Levite) WITH Aaron and his sons (priests) — but the mishna has priests and Levites watching in DIFFERENT places (3 vs. 21)!
3️⃣ Resolution: read it as two separate clauses — 'those camping...were Moses' (the Levites' watch), THEN 'Aaron and his sons, keeping the watch' (the priests', separately)

4️⃣ Since Moses keeps watch in ONE discrete place, and the verse juxtaposes Aaron/sons the same way, each of THEM also keeps watch in a discrete place — Aaron in one, his two sons together accounting for the total of three priestly posts
5️⃣ Rav Ashi's alternative: the verse repeats the root ש-מ-ר three times ('שֹׁמְרִים מִשְׁמֶרֶת...לְמִשְׁמֶרֶת') — hinting directly at three separate watches

slides.title: 🏢 Were Avtinas and HaNitzotz Real Upper Stories?
slides.subtitle: A dilemma, resolved by a parallel mishna and a verse

lines.speaker: The dilemma
lines.text: Were the chambers of Avtinas and HaNitzotz genuinely upper stories (with a separate floor below), or were they simply very tall halls — perhaps built on pillars — that merely resembled upper stories?

lines.speaker: Resolution (Middot)
lines.text: A parallel mishna about the Temple gates describes the Gate of the Spark as a portico with a true upper story built ABOVE it — priests watched from above, Levites from below. This confirms: real upper stories.

lines.speaker: Why do Levites watch from BELOW?
lines.text: A baraita derives this from Numbers 18:2 and 18:4: the Levites' role is to 'accompany' the priests in the priests' OWN watch-service — meaning they join as a secondary presence, not as equals stationed at the same height.

lines.speaker: The structural result
lines.text: Priests keep watch from the upper story; Levites keep watch from the level below — physically expressing their distinct, subordinate role in this particular shared duty.

slides.title: 🪨 Building Stone Benches Without Hammer or Ax
slides.subtitle: Reconciling Beit HaMoked's construction with the Temple's famous silence
slides.hebrewSource: וְהַבַּיִת בְּהִבָּנוֹתוֹ אֶבֶן שְׁלֵמָה ... וְלֹא נִשְׁמַע בַּבַּיִת בְּהִבָּנֹתוֹ
slides.label: The question and answer:
slides.text: The mishna describes Beit HaMoked's protruding stone rows (רוֹבְדִין) — steps of chiseled stone by which priests climbed up to a higher row where they slept. But 1 Kings 6:7 states the Temple was built of finished stone, with 'no hammer, ax, or iron tool heard' during construction — so how were these stones shaped? Abaye answers: the prohibition applied only to cutting stone WITHIN the Temple precincts. Builders instead brought pre-shaped stones — some small, some large ('stones of ten cubits and stones of eight cubits,' 1 Kings 7:10) — already finished at the quarry, using larger stones for the lower tier and smaller ones above. Separately, the Gemara explains the elders slept on these stone benches rather than bringing in beds, since bringing beds into the Temple was simply not proper conduct.

summary.principle: Every detail of the Temple's overnight watch and morning ash-removal ritual — from a private bathroom's door signal to the exact verse justifying three separate guard posts — reflects a Temple culture built on precise, textually-grounded protocol, where even stone benches had to be quarried elsewhere to preserve the sanctuary's total silence from iron tools.

quiz.q: How could a ritually impure priest travel from the Chamber of the Hearth to the immersion chamber without passing through the Temple courtyard?
o: He was carried by other priests
Through a circuitous underground passage beneath the Temple, lit by lamps on both sides
He waited outside the Temple entirely
There was no accommodation; he simply left the Temple grounds
quiz.e: The mishna describes a lamplit underground passage specifically built so an impure priest could reach the immersion chamber without entering the sacred courtyard.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, when does the appointed officer arrive to begin the ash-removal lottery?
o: Always precisely at midnight
At an unpredictable time — sometimes at the rooster's first crow, sometimes shortly before or after
Only on Shabbat
Exactly at sunrise every day
quiz.e: The mishna explicitly states that 'not all times are equal' — the officer's arrival time varies, tied loosely to the rooster's crow.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara derive from Numbers 3:38 that priests kept watch in three separate locations?
o: It cites a separate, explicit verse naming three locations

By reading the verse as describing Moses (Levites) separately from 'Aaron and his sons' (priests), with Aaron keeping watch in one place and his two sons together accounting for two more — three total; Rav Ashi alternatively notes the threefold repetition of the root for 'watch'
By counting the number of Temple gates
The three locations are not derived from any verse at all
quiz.e: The Gemara parses the verse's structure and repeated terminology to derive that Aaron and his two sons occupied three distinct guard posts, separate from the Levites' watch.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the dilemma about whether Beit Avtinas and Beit HaNitzotz were genuine upper stories?
o: It leaves the question completely unresolved (teiku)
By citing a parallel mishna (Middot) describing the Gate of the Spark with a true upper story where priests watched from above and Levites from below
By saying they were definitely not upper stories
By comparing them to the Holy of Holies
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing the mishna in Middot, which explicitly describes a genuine upper story at the Gate of the Spark, with priests above and Levites below.

quiz.q: How does Abaye reconcile Beit HaMoked's chiseled stone benches with the verse stating the Temple was built without any iron tool being heard during construction?
o: He says the verse doesn't apply to Beit HaMoked
He explains that the prohibition applied only to cutting stone WITHIN the Temple precincts; the stones were pre-shaped elsewhere at the quarry before being brought in
He says the benches were actually made of wood, not stone
He says the verse is not to be taken literally
quiz.e: Abaye clarifies that stones were shaped outside the Temple grounds at the quarry, so no iron tool was ever used or heard within the sacred precincts itself, even though the finished stones were chiseled.
